question.:question/problem: The rate at which a freshly baked cake cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let $T(t)$ be the temperature of the cake in degrees Fahrenheit, and let $t>0$ be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is ${70}^{∘}\text{F},$ which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the cake? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={70}^{∘}\text{F},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-70).
$$

generation.domain: k>0; T>ambient; all times in minutes; temperatures in one declared scale
